chapter_theme: Quarrelling with one's own heart for taking the other side. The woman charges it with disloyalty for loving him when she wants to sulk, and the chapter ends in the man's voice, on Parimelazhagar's reading, with both lovers facing the same discovery: one's own heart may not be on one's side.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1291-1298 to the woman, addressing or describing her heart, and 1299-1300 to the man, in a sulk he can't end. Manakkudavar gives 1299 to the woman.

1291.reading: The woman asks her heart why it isn't hers, when it has seen how his heart belongs to him.
1291.nuance: An elegantly sharp opening. Two hearts are compared as servants, and his has a better idea of loyalty. Parimelazhagar adds the sting: even those who can't figure out what to do can copy someone else, and the heart won't do even that.

1292.reading: The woman says that her heart, even after seeing that he isn't close to her, goes to him as if he weren't hostile.
1292.nuance: The heart's reason is the small hope, that he won't be angry. Parimelazhagar says it's relying on old familiarity, which is a thin basis, and calls it the greatest folly.

1293.reading: The woman asks her heart if it follows him as it pleases, on the principle that the ruined have no friends.
1293.nuance: A piece of proverbial wisdom about false friends, turned against the heart. By using it she also admits that she is the one ruined. Parimelazhagar glosses கெட்டார் as her loss of honour, and the verse casts her heart as a fair-weather friend.

1294.reading: The woman tells her heart that it won't first sulk and then enjoy, so no one will plan such things with it any more.
1294.nuance: It's almost comic: she drops the heart from her team as an unreliable accomplice. Sulking here is a strategy with a sequence to it, sulk first and enjoy later, and the heart can't wait.

1295.reading: The woman says her heart fears not having him and, on having him, fears parting, so it is in endless grief.
1295.nuance: In Parimelazhagar's setting she says this within the hearing of a friend who has come as an envoy, so it also means she will let him in. He observes that there is no third state, which makes this grief complete.

1296.reading: The woman says that when she sits alone and thinks of him, her heart is there only to eat her.
1296.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the irony: it stays with her only to work on her, not to help her quarrel. Manakkudavar gives this a small domestic turn: she tells the friend, 'you've come now, and so I've escaped it'.

1297.reading: The woman says that, stuck with this worthless, foolish heart that can't forget him, she has even forgotten shame.
1297.nuance: There are two forgettings in tension. Parimelazhagar's definition of shame is one of the finest things in his commentary: however long two have been together, to shrink as if seeing the other for the first time. His definition of the heart's foolishness: remembering when he's away, forgetting when he's there.

1298.reading: The woman says her heart, thinking it would be disgraceful to despise him, keeps thinking of what pertains to him, out of உயிர்க்காதல்.

positions.position: உயிர்க்காதல் means the heart loves its own life: it won't die, and so it plans reconciliation.
positions.quote: உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு - உயிர்மேல் காதலையுடைய என் நெஞ்சு

positions.position: It's a heart whose love is as dear as life, and it thinks on his greatness.

1299.reading: Who will be a companion in grief, when one's own heart is no companion? The speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
1299.nuance: If it's the man, then he has come to the state she has been in for ten verses. His heart is doing to him what hers did: urging union when he should be standing firm.

positions.position: The man speaks, in a sulk that won't yield, whose heart still wants her.
The woman replies to the friend who asks who would help.
positions.quote: இது தலைமகள் துணையாவார் யாரென்ற தோழிக்குக் கூறியது.

1300.reading: The man, for Parimelazhagar, says that it's no wonder if strangers aren't one's own, when one's own heart isn't.
1300.nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a witty aim: 'stranger' here is the sulking woman, who no longer seems his beloved, so if his own heart pains him for her sake, it's a small thing if she, a stranger, sulks. The other commentators don't name a speaker, and read it as a maxim.

links.note: 796 says ruin has one benefit: it's a measuring rod for friends. 1293 applies this proverb to one's own heart, which she treats as a friend who proves false. The inner dialogue has absorbed a whole social ethic of friendship.

In 1244 her eyes eat her alive with longing, and in 1296 her heart does. The same verb is used for what are, in effect, her own organs, and these chapters keep treating her as a person being consumed by her parts.
1247 demands that the heart give up either love or shame. 1297 tells us what happened: shame got forgotten. The chapter between them, on breaking restraint, is how.

ஏதிலர், the 'stranger', has been her word for him in the town's mouth, in 1129 and 1130. In 1300 the same word is used for a stranger, and now the one who isn't one's own is one's own heart. By the end, the outsider is inside.

source_issues: 1299: Parimelazhagar's gloss has பணை அல் வழி where the verse has துணையல் வழி, a typo.
1293: Parimelazhagar's note has a misplaced விளக்கம் inside the Kalittokai citation.
